title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants
tagline: Tissues and tissue systems, the internal plan of root, stem and leaf, and how thickness is added.

overview.intro: Anatomy is the study of internal structure, and this chapter builds it from the tissues upward: the simple and complex tissues that make up every organ, the three tissue systems, the internal arrangement of root, stem and leaf as seen in transverse section, the difference between dicot and monocot in each, and finally secondary growth, which explains how a tree gets thick. The examination is dominated by labelled transverse sections — root, stem and leaf of both a dicot and a monocot — so the differences between them are what must be held precisely.

facts.label: Simple tissues
facts.value: Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma, differing in wall thickening and the fate of the cell at maturity.

facts.label: Complex tissues
facts.value: Xylem and phloem, each made of several cell types working together as a conductive tissue.

facts.label: Duct arrangement
facts.value: Dicot stem has a ring of vascular bundles; monocot stem has scattered bundles; the root has a radial arrangement in both.

facts.label: Secondary growth
facts.value: The vascular cambium adds xylem inward and phloem outward, and the cork cambium replaces the epidermis with periderm.

learningOutcomes: Distinguish the three simple tissues and the two complex tissues by structure and function.
Describe the tissue systems of the plant body.
Compare the internal anatomy of dicot and monocot root, stem and leaf.
Explain the position and activity of the vascular and cork cambia.
Relate secondary growth to annual rings and the formation of bark.

blocks.text: Plant tissues are of two kinds. Simple tissues are made of one kind of cell and are of three types. Parenchyma is the most common: thin-walled, living cells with intercellular spaces that store food and water and can divide to heal a wound; the chlorenchyma form carries chloroplasts and photosynthesises, while aerenchyma has large air cavities that keep aquatic plants afloat. Collenchyma consists of living cells with unevenly thickened walls of cellulose and pectin, concentrated just beneath the epidermis of a young stem or leaf, where it provides flexibility and tensile strength without rigidity — it is what lets a stalk bend without snapping. Sclerenchyma is the opposite in every respect: dead at maturity, with a uniformly thick secondary wall lignified so hard that the cell cannot function, providing mechanical support and stiffness; its fibres are long and bundled, as in jute and flax, and its sclereids or stone cells are short and give the grit of a pear. Complex tissues are made of several kinds of cell acting together, and there are two. Xylem conducts water and minerals upward and gives mechanical support, and it contains four elements: tracheids, which are long tapering cells with lignified, pitted walls that conduct and support; vessels, wider tubes formed from dead cells joined end to end with the end walls dissolved away so the column is open; xylem parenchyma, the only living element, which stores food; and xylem fibres, which support. All the conducting elements are dead at maturity, which is important — the tube is a physical pipe, not a living pump. Phloem translocates organic food in both directions and contains sieve tubes, long cells joined by sieve plates with pores through which the cytoplasm streams, companion cells that control the sieve tube and keep it alive, phloem parenchyma for storage, and phloem fibres for support. The sieve tube element loses its nucleus at maturity yet stays alive because the companion cell, with its dense cytoplasm and organelles, supplies it. Together these tissues are arranged into three systems: the epidermal system, the outer protective covering with its cuticle, stomata and hairs; the ground or fundamental system of cortex and pith, which stores and photosynthesises; and the vascular system of xylem and phloem, which conducts. Every organ is built from these three, which is why anatomy becomes a matter of arrangement rather than of new material.

items: Parenchyma: thin-walled living storage and photosynthetic cells with intercellular spaces.
Collenchyma: living, unevenly thickened, flexible support beneath the epidermis.
Sclerenchyma: dead with lignified walls, giving rigid support; fibres and sclereids.
Xylem: tracheids, vessels, parenchyma and fibres, the conducting elements dead at maturity.
Phloem: sieve tubes, companion cells, parenchyma and fibres, with the sieve element alive but enucleate.
Companion cells keep the sieve tube element supplied and controlled.
Epidermal system protects; ground system stores and photosynthesises; vascular system conducts.
Every organ comprises all three tissue systems in a characteristic arrangement.

items.note: Clusters of thick-walled sclereids, the stone cells, are what the teeth encounter — a tissue visible without a microscope.
Strings of collenchyma under the surface give strength with flexibility, so the stalk yields rather than breaks.

learn.title: The internal anatomy of root, stem and leaf

blocks.text: Each organ has a characteristic arrangement of its tissue systems, and the differences between dicot and monocot are consistent enough to be tested directly. In the dicot root, seen in transverse section, the outermost layer is the epidermis with root hairs for absorption, and beneath it lies the cortex of parenchyma with no hypodermis and no endodermis at first — though a mature root has an endodermis, the innermost cortex layer with Casparian strips of suberin that force water to cross a membrane rather than pass between cells, followed by a pericycle from which lateral roots arise. Vascular tissue is radial: xylem lies in an arm-shaped, often diarch to tetrarch mass in the centre with patches of phloem alternating between the arms, and there is no pith in a dicot root. In the monocot root the same plan holds but with a ring of many vascular bundles around a central pith, and the xylem is polyarch. In the dicot stem the arrangement changes completely: beneath the epidermis lies a hypodermis of collenchyma, then a wide cortex of parenchyma, an endodermis with starch sheath, a pericycle, and then vascular bundles arranged in a ring — each bundle conjoint and open, with phloem outside, a strip of fascicular cambium between, and xylem inside, with a medullary ray of parenchyma between neighbouring bundles. Pith and medulla occupy the centre, and medullary rays carry materials sideways. In the monocot stem the vascular bundles are scattered throughout the ground tissue rather than in a ring, each is conjoint and closed — with no cambium, so it cannot grow thick — and the epidermis is often thickened with silica. The leaf shows a third pattern: the epidermis above and below with a cuticle and stomata mainly on the lower surface, the mesophyll between them differentiated in a dicot into palisade parenchyma of columnar cells packed with chloroplasts for light capture and spongy parenchyma with large air spaces for gas exchange, and vascular bundles, or veins, of xylem above and phloem below running through it. A monocot leaf has undifferentiated mesophyll with no palisade, and many grasses have their stomata on both surfaces with bulliform cells on the upper epidermis that let the leaf roll inward in dry weather to reduce water loss. These differences are what a drawing question examines, so they are worth memorising as paired contrasts: ring against scattered bundles, open against closed, palisade against uniform mesophyll.

items: Dicot root: epidermis with root hairs, cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle, radial vascular tissue and no pith.
Monocot root: polyarch xylem in a ring around a central pith.
Dicot stem: hypodermis of collenchyma, cortex, endodermis, and vascular bundles in a ring, conjoint and open.
Monocot stem: vascular bundles scattered, conjoint and closed with no cambium.
Endodermis with Casparian strips controls the entry of water into the vascular cylinder.
Pericycle gives rise to lateral roots in the root.
Dicot leaf: palisade and spongy mesophyll, stomata mainly below, xylem above phloem in the vein.
Monocot leaf: undifferentiated mesophyll, sometimes stomata on both surfaces, bulliform cells for rolling.

items.text: Why a monocot stem never thickens
items.note: Its bundles are closed — no cambium — so no new xylem or phloem can be added and the stem stays the same width.
Water reaching the endodermis must cross the selectively permeable membrane, so the plant controls what enters the xylem.

learn.title: Secondary growth: how a stem becomes thick

blocks.text: Secondary growth is the increase in girth produced by lateral meristems, and it is absent from most monocots because they lack the necessary cambia. The vascular cambium is a cylinder of meristematic cells lying between the xylem and phloem; it arises partly from the strips of fascicular cambium between the bundles and partly from the medullary rays between them, which together join into a continuous ring. When it divides, cells cut inward become secondary xylem and cells cut outward become secondary phloem, so the stem thickens on both sides of the ring while the original primary xylem and phloem are pushed outward. Because the cambium is more active in the growing season, the xylem produced in spring is wide-lumened and light while that produced later is narrow and dense, and the contrast between successive years produces the concentric annual rings visible in a cut trunk — which is how the age of a tree can be counted and how a wet or dry year is recorded in the wood. The cells of the secondary xylem are the timber: dead, thick-walled and lignified, they give wood its strength, and the difference between sapwood, which still conducts, and heartwood, which is filled with resins and no longer conducts, is one of age and function. As the stem expands the outer tissues cannot stretch, so they split, and a second lateral meristem, the cork cambium or phellogen, arises in the cortex or hypodermis. It divides to produce cork cells outward, which are dead, suberised and waterproof as they mature and form the protective periderm replacing the epidermis, and phelloderm inward. The whole outer covering of a woody stem — periderm plus the remains of older phloem — is what is called bark, and the small pores visible on it are lenticels, areas of loosely arranged cells that allow gas exchange through the otherwise impermeable cork. Without cork cambium and periderm a thickening stem would be left with a cracked, unprotected surface; with them the tree carries its own waterproof, insulating and pathogen-resistant coat, renewed each year from within.

items: Secondary growth is the increase in girth from lateral meristems and is absent from most monocots.

items.note: Each pair of light and dark rings is one year: a wide light ring means a wet growing season and a good year.
The cork cambium lays down a new layer each year while the older, outer phloem is stretched and shed.

learn.title: The comparisons that carry the marks

blocks.text: Anatomy is examined through comparison, and six contrasts account for most of the marks available. Dicot root against monocot root: the dicot has a diarch to tetrarch mass of xylem in the centre with no pith, while the monocot has a ring of many, polyarch, bundles around a pith; both have radial vascular tissue, an endodermis with Casparian strips and a pericycle. Dicot stem against monocot stem: bundles in a ring against scattered, open against closed, a distinct cortex and pith against undifferentiated ground tissue, and hypodermis of collenchyma in the dicot against sclerenchyma or thickened epidermis in many monocots. Dicot leaf against monocot leaf: reticulate against parallel veins, differentiated palisade and spongy mesophyll against uniform mesophyll, stomata mainly below against on both surfaces in many grasses, and often bulliform cells that let the blade roll. Xylem against phloem: dead conducting elements against living ones, water and minerals upward against food in both directions, lignified walls against cellulose walls with sieve plates. Apoplast against symplast: the wall pathway against the cytoplasmic pathway, blocked at the endodermis against continuous through plasmodesmata. Primary against secondary growth: increase in length from apical meristems against increase in girth from lateral meristems, producing primary tissues against producing wood and bark. The method of answering is the same in every case: give the feature as a row, place each organ in its column, and then add one sentence stating what the difference achieves — a closed bundle means no thickening, a differentiated mesophyll means specialised light capture, dead xylem elements mean an unbroken pipe. The reason is what separates a listed table from a full-marks one, and it is always a consequence of the structure rather than a new fact.

items: Dicot root: tetrarch xylem with no pith; monocot root: polyarch ring around a pith.
Dicot stem: bundles in a ring and open; monocot stem: scattered and closed.
Dicot leaf: palisade and spongy mesophyll with reticulate veins; monocot: uniform mesophyll and parallel veins.
Xylem: dead lignified elements carrying water upward; phloem: living sieve tubes carrying food both ways.
Apoplast is blocked by the Casparian strip; symplast continues through plasmodesmata.
Primary growth adds length from apical meristems; secondary growth adds girth from cambia.
Every comparison row should be closed with the consequence of the structure.

keyPoints: Parenchyma stores, collenchyma supports flexibly, sclerenchyma supports rigidly and is dead at maturity.
Xylem conducts water with tracheids and vessels and supports with fibres.
Phloem conducts food through sieve tubes kept alive by companion cells.
The epidermal, ground and vascular tissue systems build every organ.
The endodermis with Casparian strips controls entry into the vascular cylinder.
The dicot root has radial vascular tissue and no pith; the monocot root is polyarch with a pith.
The dicot stem has bundles in a ring, conjoint and open; the monocot stem has scattered closed bundles.
The dicot leaf has palisade and spongy mesophyll; the monocot leaf mesophyll is undifferentiated.

questions.prompt: Which tissue is dead at maturity and has uniformly lignified walls?
questions.explanation: Sclerenchyma dies when its secondary wall is deposited, leaving rigid support.

questions.explanation: Monocot bundles lie scattered through the ground tissue and lack cambium, so they are closed.

questions.explanation: The suberin band in the endodermis forces water to cross a membrane before entering the xylem.

Phloem is laid down in rings
questions.answer: Spring wood has wide vessels and late wood narrow ones
questions.explanation: The vascular cambium is more active in spring, so each year gives a light wide-vessel band and a dark narrow one.

questions.prompt: The lateral meristem that produces secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward is the __________ cambium.
questions.explanation: It forms a continuous ring from the fascicular cambium and the medullary rays.

questions.prompt: The protective outer covering of a woody stem, formed of periderm and old phloem, is called the __________.
questions.explanation: Lenticels in the bark allow gas exchange through the otherwise waterproof cork.

questions.answer: Parenchyma consists of thin-walled living cells with cellulose walls and intercellular spaces, found throughout the plant in the pith, cortex and mesophyll; it stores food and water, its chlorenchyma form photosynthesises, and it can divide to heal wounds or form a callus. Sclerenchyma consists of cells with uniformly thickened secondary walls heavily lignified, and the cells are dead at maturity with no protoplast; it provides rigid mechanical support and protection, and it occurs as long fibres in jute and flax and as short sclereids or stone cells that give the grit of a pear.
questions.explanation: Contrast wall thickness, living or dead state, function and location.

questions.prompt: How does the arrangement of vascular bundles differ between a dicot and a monocot stem?
questions.answer: In a dicot stem the vascular bundles are arranged in a regular ring near the periphery, separated by medullary rays of parenchyma, and each bundle is conjoint and open — the phloem lies outward, a strip of fascicular cambium lies between it and the xylem, and the xylem lies inward. The presence of that cambium means secondary growth is possible, which is why dicot stems thicken. In a monocot stem the vascular bundles are scattered through the whole ground tissue with no regular arrangement, and each is conjoint and closed, lacking any cambial strip, so no secondary xylem or phloem can be added and the stem does not increase in girth. The monocot ground tissue is also less clearly differentiated into cortex and pith than that of the dicot.
questions.explanation: Ring against scattered arrangement, open against closed bundles, and the consequence for secondary growth.

questions.prompt: State the functions of the three tissue systems of a plant.
questions.answer: The epidermal tissue system is the outer covering, comprising the epidermis with its cuticle, stomata and hairs; it protects the underlying tissues, reduces water loss through the cuticle, and allows gas exchange and transpiration through the guard cells of the stomata. The ground or fundamental tissue system consists of the cortex, pith and mesophyll; it carries out photosynthesis where it contains chloroplasts and stores food and water elsewhere, and in the stem it provides packing and some support. The vascular tissue system contains the xylem and phloem; xylem conducts water and minerals upward from the roots and gives mechanical support, while phloem translocates organic food in both directions between the leaves and the rest of the plant.
questions.explanation: All three systems with what each is composed of and what it does.

questions.prompt: Describe the process of secondary growth in a dicot stem and explain how bark and annual rings are formed.
questions.answer: Secondary growth begins with the vascular cambium, a lateral meristem that becomes active between the primary xylem and phloem. Part of it comes from the strips of fascicular cambium already present in each vascular bundle, and part from the parenchyma of the medullary rays between the bundles; these join up to form a continuous ring of meristematic cells. Once active, the cambium divides periclinally: cells cut towards the inside differentiate as secondary xylem, and cells cut towards the outside become secondary phloem, so the stem increases in diameter on both sides while the primary xylem and phloem are displaced outward and the pith is compressed at the centre. The cambium is not equally active through the year — in the spring, with abundant water, it produces xylem with wide vessels and thin walls, giving light-coloured spring wood, while later in the season it produces narrow, thick-walled elements forming dark late wood. One light band and one dark band together make an annual ring, and because a new ring is added each year the concentric pattern records the age of the tree and the conditions of each season. As the diameter grows, the epidermis and cortex cannot stretch and they rupture, so a second lateral meristem, the cork cambium, arises in the cortex or hypodermis. It divides to produce cork cells outward — dead, suberised and waterproof at maturity — and phelloderm inward; the cork, the cork cambium and the phelloderm together form the periderm, which replaces the epidermis as the protective covering. Lenticels, gaps of loosely arranged thin-walled cells in the periderm, allow gases to reach the living tissues beneath. Bark consists of the periderm together with the phloem and cortex lying outside the vascular cambium, and it is shed and renewed as the stem grows, which is why a tree carries a thick, fissured, protective coat.
questions.explanation: Both cambia in order, what each produces and the direction, the seasonal origin of rings, the rupture of the outer tissues and the formation of periderm, lenticels and bark.

questions.prompt: A transverse section shows a stem with vascular bundles scattered through the ground tissue, each bundle with xylem and phloem but no cambium between them. Identify whether the plant is a dicot or a monocot and justify each feature, and state one consequence of what you observe.
questions.answer: The features identify the specimen as a monocot stem. The first is the arrangement of the vascular bundles: they lie scattered through the ground tissue rather than in a regular ring, which is the monocot condition, whereas a dicot stem shows its bundles in a single ring with medullary rays between them. The second is the absence of cambium between the xylem and the phloem in each bundle — the bundle is closed rather than open. In a dicot each bundle is conjoint and open, with a strip of fascicular cambium that continues into the medullary rays to form a continuous ring of vascular cambium, and it is that tissue that produces secondary xylem and phloem. Third, the ground tissue is not clearly differentiated into cortex, endodermis and pith as it is in a dicot, but grades from the epidermis to the centre, which again follows the monocot plan. The consequence of the closed bundles is that no secondary growth can occur: without cambium no new vascular tissue can be added, so the stem cannot increase in girth and remains a slender, non-woody axis for the life of the plant. That is why monocots such as grasses and palms have slender stems — palms add no girth after the initial growth — and why the mechanical strength they do have comes from sclerenchyma bundles and silica rather than from wood.
questions.explanation: Both monocot features identified with the dicot contrast, then the consequence for secondary growth and stem form.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of the dicot leaf is adapted to the two jobs of photosynthesis and gas exchange.
questions.answer: A dicot leaf is thin and flat, which gives a large surface area for intercepting light while keeping the diffusion path to the interior short, and its internal structure divides the work between two layers of mesophyll. The upper epidermis is a single layer of transparent cells with a cuticle that lets light through while limiting water loss, and beneath it the palisade parenchyma consists of columnar cells packed closely together and loaded with chloroplasts that are shifted towards the upper surface to intercept the strongest light — this layer does most of the photosynthesis. Below it the spongy parenchyma has irregular cells with large intercellular air spaces continuous with each other and with the stomatal pores, so carbon dioxide reaching a stoma diffuses rapidly through the spaces to every photosynthetic cell, and the oxygen produced diffuses out by the same route. Gas exchange itself is regulated by the stomata, each a pore between two kidney-shaped guard cells that contain chloroplasts and control the opening: when the guard cells take up water they become turgid and bow apart, opening the pore, and when they lose water the pore closes. Most dicot leaves carry stomata predominantly on the lower surface, which reduces water loss because the upper surface receives direct sun and would warm the pore and dry the leaf. Veins run through the mesophyll with xylem above and phloem below, delivering water to replace that lost by transpiration and carrying away the sugars as they are made — so the leaf photosynthesises, exchanges gases, loses water in a controlled way, and transports its products, with the structure of each layer matched to its part in that work.
questions.explanation: Flat shape, transparent epidermis, palisade for light capture, spongy spaces for diffusion, stomatal control and positioning, and the vein supply.
